extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy, and the theory of reasoning
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and evaluating principles about syllogistic reasoning, the role and form of general propositions, the nature of axioms and hypotheses, and inductive methods as discussed in a philosophical/textbook treatment of logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantification of the predicate
rubrics_metrics.description: The quantification of the predicate (making the predicate a class-name and quantifying it) is superfluous and erroneous; it does not express what is in the mind of the speaker when he enunciates the proposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example/argument: Saying 'All men are mortal' affirms the attribute mortality of all men without thinking of the class 'mortal' in the concrete. Quantifying the predicate leads the mind out of the proposition into another order of ideas and is only appropriate for artificial purposes where the predicate is to be treated as a class-name. See discussion contrasting ordinary form vs. Hamilton's doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositions should reflect mental content of the speaker
rubrics_metrics.description: A correct logical form should express what is actually in the mind of the person who asserts the proposition rather than an artificial class-based form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a logical reformulation (e.g., quantifying predicates) is not what the speaker mentally posits when asserting, it is misleading. Logical formulations must preserve the mental content and not introduce extraneous class-thinking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of general terms and attributes
rubrics_metrics.description: General names denote resemblances of our sensations (or other feelings); attributes are precisely those similarities. A general conception is 'the One in the Many' — the common something which gives a meaning to the general name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: If a general conception were considered as many different conceptions for each individual, general language would be impossible. The general term 'man' connotes the general type of sensations derived from all men and the power to produce sensations of that type. Thus attributes should be conceived as one common resemblance, not numerically many.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-existence in axioms means joint attribution, not simultaneity
rubrics_metrics.description: When the axiom speaks of the co-existence of two things with the same third, it refers to being jointly attributes of the same subject rather than simultaneous existence in time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: The attribute 'being born without teeth' and 'having thirty-two teeth in mature age' are co-existent as attributes of 'man' even though they never exist simultaneously in the same individual. Avoid interpreting 'co-exist' as temporal simultaneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: A logical axiom must accommodate partial vs total coincidence (need for limitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: An axiom used as a basis for syllogism must allow for the distinction between total and partial coincidence of terms; it must provide a means of limiting transfers through the middle term when terms are not co-extensive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bain's criticism: an axiom that simply states 'A carries B; B carries C; therefore A carries C' risks implying co-extensiveness. The axiom must account for the fact that A may carry B 'in common with other things', and similar qualification must be transferrable so as not to force erroneous universal inferences. Practical safeguards include teaching conversion and ordinary language sense of 'mark'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer practical formulations of axioms to avoid misinterpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use practical, behaviourally clear forms of axioms (e.g., 'Nota notæ est nota rei ipsius') to exclude misinterpretations that could arise from literal or ambiguous wording.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The practical form prevents mistakes like inferring reciprocity ('if a is a mark of b, b can never exist without a') by grounding the axiom in ordinary usage and warning against literal misreadings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different axioms serve different logical aims (formal consistency vs pursuit of truth)
rubrics_metrics.description: The dictum de omni is appropriate as the fundamental axiom for the logic of mere consistency (Formal Logic), while the proposed axiom (co-existence-based) is more suitable for the logic of the pursuit of truth by deduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both forms have value and place: retain dictum de omni for formal logical consistency; adopt the co-existence axiom when emphasizing conditions that make deductive reasoning a road to truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of major and minor premises: interpretative and precautionary, not essential conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Major and minor premises, as formally stated in the syllogism, are not necessary conditions of reasoning; they serve to interpret general statements and to act as a precaution against erroneous inference. Reasoning fundamentally proceeds from particulars to particulars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The only minor really needed is that the new individual is like the observed individuals. Syllogistic majors/minors 'start into existence together' as a way of revising and expressing an already existing inference from particulars. They do not add evidence but improve clarity and guard against error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressing general propositions to reflect inductive origin ('Any' vs 'All')
rubrics_metrics.description: General propositions used in reasoning from experience are better phrased in the form 'Any man is mortal' rather than 'All men are mortal' to manifest that inductive reasoning proceeds from particulars to particulars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mode shows that general propositions vouch for the legitimacy of inferences from observed individuals to unobserved ones; it avoids implying that general statements are prior proofs of particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of hypotheses and definitions in geometry: known fictions/approximations
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypotheses in geometry and definitions are assumptions known not to be literally true; their hypothetical element consists in assuming exactitude where only approximation is available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that definitions (e.g., of a straight line) idealize and approximate experience. The hypothetical device permits reasoning about ideal limits; call this device a fiction or hypothesis but be explicit about the assumptions involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inductive proof by approximation (Method of Concomitant Variations / limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Axioms of geometry (and other sciences) can be justified inductively by proof by approximation: observing gradations approaching an ideal limit supports the axiom in the limit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Though we never experience perfectly straight, breadthless lines, we observe lines with decreasing breadth/flexure; as their properties approach the ideal, the space-inclosing tendency approaches zero. This is an instance of the Method of Concomitant Variations and corresponds to the mathematical doctrine of limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental experience (contemplation/recollection) counts as part of evidence for axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: Experience, as relevant to axioms, includes mental contemplation and vivid recollection; imagined or recollected mental pictures can serve in place of immediate external impressions when judging simple geometrical relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: Primary relations (like straightness) can be vividly called up by the imagination and used as evidence. Individuals differ in vividness of recollection, but for simple geometrical forms most people form distinct mental images which justify reasoning from them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for recognizing axiomatic truths: continual, simple, uncontradicted experience
rubrics_metrics.description: A truth that is necessary and universal and expressed in simple axiomatic form will be continually suggested by experience, verified in every instance of the object, and thus command implicit assent; its simplicity and ubiquity make its verification obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If experience repeatedly and consistently suggests a proposition, and it is simple and clear, it becomes a recognized axiom. Violation of such axioms renders many propositions inconceivable. Use the ubiquity and simplicity of experiential suggestion as tests for axiomatic status.
